utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would call the case for hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-01-42-T, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The first Prosecution witness to call would be Mr. Paul Davies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could be affirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would be seated, please. Ms. Somers. Examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you give your complete and full name, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: My name is Paul Davies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, I think for the sake of time, I'm going to lead you through a little bit of the background. But you are or have been for some period of time associated with ITN. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is ITN?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Independent Television News. It's the news network of ITV, which is the commercial television network in the UK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is it based?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It's based in London.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your current position and what have been your positions up to now with ITN?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I'm a senior news correspondent at ITN. Until recently I was an international correspondent, specialising in areas of conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you begin your employ with ITN?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the conflicts you have been covering for ITN include?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Dozens. Gulf war, Iran-Iraq War, Kurdistan --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak of the conflicts, could you give a time frame, the years in which...?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Sure. Most of the serious conflicts in the world from 1985 through until recently, 2001, 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among that conflict coverage, was the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That was a large part of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your time in Dubrovnik, would you give us, please, the range of time you were there.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes. I was there from October the 31st, to November the 21st.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what year, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Of those -- three weeks -- in 1990. Was it? Was it 1990 or 1991. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then your answer -- do I understand you correctly, you're talking about 1991, the period of conflict?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment as I understand it, it's 1990 or 1991, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure thinking about it it's 1991. It's just not one of those things that you pin down too often. I remember the days and the weeks and the months, maybe not the number of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we will settle for 1991 as your preferred year at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the year that Dubrovnik was under siege and the conflict was going on there, and 1991 would be that year, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What brought you in? What was your brief or your mission in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The mission was to try and get inside into what was developing as a siege. It had been developing for some time. We had been aware of it. I had been working in other parts of the former Yugoslavia and I was asked would I try to get into Dubrovnik and actually be on the inside of what appeared to be developing into an interesting situation there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: By sea. We flew from London to Austria, travelled over land to Rijeka and caught a fast ferry boat from Rijeka. We were aware that a flotilla of boats were attempting to break the blockade, setting out from Split and we tried to join up with them and succeeded in joining up with them just outside the fortress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attempt to go by automobile?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We didn't but many other teams had done so. It wasn't -- it was no longer possible to go by ordinary legitimate routes, whether it was by road or by water or by air. All of the normal routes into Dubrovnik had been cut by the military situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Again, you were unable to travel by auto because of...?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Because the roads were blocked by fighting, and when they weren't blocked by fighting they were blocked by military roadblocks. These could be from the various factions that were involved in it, but certainly before you got into Dubrovnik there were roadblocks set up by the JNA, the Yugoslavian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you got to Dubrovnik, where were you accommodated?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We lived in a hotel, called the Argentina hotel. It was the hotel alongside the Old Town and the hotel that was used by the European Community monitoring people and by a number of diplomats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with a body of persons called the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We had regular contact with them. They had their base, their headquarters, in the same hotel, and we would meet them on a daily basis, both in the course of our work but also socially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the duration of your stay in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Three weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From -- can you give a time frame?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: From the 31st of October through to the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I note that in your statement on page 2, just for correction, it says at the bottom that: "We reached Dubrovnik on 31st December." Is that a typographical error? Should that have read October?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That should read October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Dubrovnik, can you describe what the general mood of the city was. And I speak of Dubrovnik city as including all parts thereof.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I think fearful, concerned, already feeling the effects of the blockade that was stopping supplies of food getting through. There were problems with water already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of problems with water?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: People were having difficulty. A lot of the normal methods of getting water had stopped due to military action, we were told, in areas that were now no longer under the control of the Croatian authorities and some of the water supplies that had obviously come in from those areas had been stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about food?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Food was so short that they were starting rationing, distributing food to the civilian population. I remember there were also problems with power. The electricity wasn't working some of the time, and where possible, people were using generators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an area of Dubrovnik known as the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you become familiar with the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I had actually been there, oddly enough, as a holidaymaker many years before. I had visited it once working before when there had been a serious earthquake in former Yugoslavia and I had gone there to cover the effects of that. But on this occasion, we were -- the hotel where we were living was a very short walk from the Old Town. We could see the Old Town from the hotel and we visited it on a daily basis. It was one of the main reasons that we were actually there. At that stage, the fighting in and around Dubrovnik was not on a large scale, compared to what was happening else where in former Yugoslavia, places like Vukovar. But there was a huge interest in Dubrovnik in the United Kingdom, because it was one of the parts of former Yugoslavia that was known to many people because it was a popular holiday resort and a very well-known cultural site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you arrived in Dubrovnik was it still a popular holiday resort and cultural -- holiday resort? To preface the question.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No, I didn't see tourists. The blockade had already been on for some weeks by the time that we arrived and I didn't see any tourists during the time we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, when you think of the Old Town, would most prominently come to your mind? What is it about the Old Town that was attractive to the British tourist crowd?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It's a perfectly preserved medieval fortress. It's a stunning old castle, the type that you would normally see around the world in a wrecked form as opposed to a preserved form. It was also -- it was, is quite unique in that as well as being a stunning ancient monument, it's lived in. It's a living structure as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: People live in the Old City, within the walls there are homes, shops, cafes. It isn't just a tourist site that people get bussed into. I mean, there are -- there is a population there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were there, how would you characterise that population?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Well, the population was still there, but they were extremely fearful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me be more clear. Was it -- were these regular people, were they civilians? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: In the most part, they were regular people. They were the people who had lived there before, their numbers swollen slightly by refugees, people who had come in from outside to escape the fighting. There were a small number of military people as well in and around the area. But the vast majority of the people, certainly in the Old Town, were the people who had always lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I to understand are you speaking of --

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I'm talking about a civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Inasmuch as you indicated that there was conflict already in progress, did you see anything in the Old Town that suggested some preparation to meet the eventualities of conflict, anything that was done for protective purposes perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The only thing I can think of that'll answer that question would be -- an underground shelter had been prepared within the walls of the Old City and people -- a large number of people did gather there at times of shelling, bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything you might have observed about the structures, the buildings, the monuments you referred to, was there anything protective that you may have observed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Protective, as in the form of protecting against attack, not really. Certainly there was no -- there was nothing military there that would do that. In many ways, the thing that appeared to be there to protect the city, if only symbolically as it turned out, was the flags, there were flags flying over the city, very visible, very large, almost unreally large flags flying over the city, pale blue with the United Nations motif on them, but basically saying, from the first time you saw them that this is a protected site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of an organisation called UNESCO?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I have and I believe that these were the flags I'm referring to, belonging to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the presence of anyone from UNESCO in Dubrovnik during your time period there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I was aware that there were people and I believe that they were staying at the hotel, the same hotel that I was at. I had no contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How -- now, you said -- did I understand you correctly that you on a daily basis were in the Old Town during your time period there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I would think that in the 21, 22 days that I was there, there were probably only one or two days that I didn't spend some time in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you discuss what you've referred to in your statements as the "ramparts". What is it about the ramparts of the Old Town that was either useful to you or interesting to you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Useful to us was the vantage position that they offered. They were designed to give whoever was defending the Old Town a view over the surrounding area and to offer them some protection as well with the walls. And they gave them exactly that same view and degree of protection to a cameraman who was trying to see as best he could what was happening without exposing himself too much. We were using them because they gave us just about the best view of the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your time in Dubrovnik, did you have an opportunity to look carefully at the various locations in the city, and if you did, did you ever observe anything that could be classified as a military position in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you didn't what?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I didn't, sorry. Yes, I was in a position to have observed military positions, had they been there. I didn't, at any time, witness anything that I would call a military position, not even men with rifles or anything of that smaller nature on the ramparts. I didn't see weapons. The only time that I possibly saw weapons during all that time in the Old Town - and again, I stress possibly, because it's difficult to be exact - was possibly pistols being carried by an occasional person who was armed in amongst the civilians in the town. But certainly on the ramparts anything that you would call military position where you would be firing out from the city, no, I saw nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you saw nothing that would be classified as heavy weaponry in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I saw nothing that could be classified as heavy weaponry in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your time in Dubrovnik, did you personally ever observe any outgoing fire from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. I didn't observe outgoing fire from the Old Town. I observed outgoing fire occasionally, but never from the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a point during your stay when the Old Town came under shelling?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When would you be able to pinpoint the first time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The first time that I was really aware would have been the -- I think it was the 10th of November. It was the second day, I believe, of the sustained period of four days that Dubrovnik came under attack. And on that day, if I remember rightly, a number of mortars fell into the city. This was before the much, much larger attack on the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of -- excuse me, I'll rephrase that. I withdraw that. Would you discuss, please, what happened in the Old Town upon the shelling commencing. What was the reaction? Was there an expectation or an anticipation that the Old Town would be shelled?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No, there was not an expectation. I think it's fair to say there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was always a fear that the fighting might spread to the Old Town, but generally there was a belief that people were hanging on to that the Old Town would be spared, and I think that was characterised by the number of people who would come in from the modern parts of Dubrovnik into the Old Town during the worst periods of shelling, thinking that they were going to be safer there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an understanding that there might have been a safe climate in the Old Town, and if so, what was it based on?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: There was an understanding, a belief, that it would be safe. And I can only say it was built on a belief that people held. I don't know that it was necessarily any agreement that was written anywhere, but there was certainly a belief that this was a protected area, it wouldn't be attacked and they would be safe if they were there. I also, if it's helpful, in talking to some of the people that were defending Dubrovnik, got from them a sense that they wouldn't take weapons into the Old City or do anything from the Old City, because that might put at risk what they saw as the protected status of the Old City.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn of the presence of refugees in the Old City, additional population to the native population?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I saw refugees in the Old City. I wasn't aware -- I didn't know for sure that they were living there permanently. I saw them there on a number of occasions, mostly in the underground shelters. I don't know whether they were actually living there. I know various spaces that refugees were living, but at the time that I saw refugees in the Old City, they were in the underground shelter and I don't know whether that was a temporary home or permanent home for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about, to your knowledge, if you have it, of the presence of refugees in the municipal areas surrounding the Old Town? Was there a refugee population that you had become aware of?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, there was a sizeable refugee population. Most of them were being housed in the hotel that no longer had tourists to look out for them. Notably the Belvedere Hotel, which was just along the coast from the Argentina where I was staying, had a large number of refugees there and I was aware of other hotels having refugees. And indeed my own hotel became busier with refugees as some of the other hotels that the refugees were initially housed in were damaged by shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any observations about the age or anything about the condition of the refugees you may have seen?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The majority of the refugees that we saw were -- well, they were civilians, they were elderly or women and children. There didn't seem to be amongst the refugees that we saw, a sizeable number of men. I don't know the explanation of that, but the refugees that we saw being housed was because they were being given priority. I don't know -- the old, the young and particularly women with children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of any of the housing or hotels accommodating the refugee population coming under fire from the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. We visited two hotels in the early part of our stay that had been hit by shelling, and we saw refugees there who had survived the shelling. And later, during the greater onslaught, after the 9th of November when the Belvedere Hotel was hit and practically destroyed, a number of the refugees who had been staying there moved down the coast to the hotel where we were staying and were living in the corridors and various areas of our hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your own hotel, the Argentina, was there any sense that because it housed internationals it would enjoy any particular protected status?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was certainly a hope that it would do from those that were living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that hope materialise?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No, it didn't. It was also struck. We did believe that it would be one of the last places to be attacked. It was one of the reasons why we lived there. There were a number of flags flying over it, again, there was an UN flag. There was the flag that the monitors were using. There was also a British flag; it was being used as the -- as a temporary consulate by the British consul.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor, when you discuss the events of 8th November, 1991, you make a comment about a location called Srdj. What was Srdj?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Srdj was a -- well, it's a large hill, a mountain, that overlooks the Old Town of Dubrovnik. It has on it an old Napoleonic fort and this became very a strategically important site during the siege. It was held by the Croatians, and because it quite literally looked down over the Old Town - you could see it was like looking down on a street plan - whoever held it virtually held the city or certainly had the Old Town in its -- in their grasp. And therefore, it came under sustained attack over a number of days. We visited it on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with another area called Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Zarkovica is another mountain, a very large hill. It is to the south of Dubrovnik, just down the coast from the Hotel Argentina, which means it's also very close to the Old Town. And it had already been captured by the JNA. And they had a number of heavy guns on the top of it. Most of the time that we were there, it was the main position that the gunfire we were aware of was coming from into Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to visit Zarkovica during your time there or go behind JNA lines during your time there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No, we weren't. There was a road that led straight from the Hotel Argentina in that direction, but there was firing on it. It wasn't a safe road. And from time to time there was sniper fire down onto the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming from which positions, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: From the JNA positions. It was very difficult, if not impossible to work out what the policy was, because a lot of the time there wouldn't be sniper fire and then there would. And certainly a journalist friend of mine was shot outside the Hotel Argentina and had to be evacuated, and people didn't go up that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any military activity between those two mountains, Srdj and Zarkovica? If so, can you discuss it, please?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: There certainly was military activity. A lot of it seemed to be happening at night. A lot of gunfire, we could see a lot of tracer fire, the glowing rounds that you see going through the night sky. We knew of people who died -- who went off to fight or protect or whatever that area and didn't come back after some of this fighting during the night. It was a disputed area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The weaponry on these two high points, do you have any knowledge what type of weaponry was at the disposal of the Croatians on Srdj?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I went up there a couple of times, and I know what I saw, and I saw predominantly people with rifles. I did see one, at least one, heavy machine-gun that the Croatians had. I also saw some, what I would call, smaller mortars compared to some of the others that were used in the area. There were also in the hands of the Croatians. And at times they had them on Srdj and at times they moved them to other positions. They tried to keep them very mobile so they wouldn't be targets. As far as Zarkovica is concerned you could see the barrels of artillery pieces and I believe there were also tents up there, but certainly we could see the barrels of artillery pieces on top of Zarkovica. And at times of shelling, you could film those and see them recoil and the puff of smoke that came from them as they were firing. And then a few seconds later there would be an explosion in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to compare the weaponry that the Croatians had, the defenders on Srdj had, with the weaponry available to the JNA forces on Zarkovica, to give your assessment of it, if you would like to tell us?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I'm not a military expert, but you didn't need to be a military expert to see that it was completely one-sided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That one side had heavy artillery, tanks, planes, warships. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which side would that be?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That was the JNA. And the other side, the Croatians, had mostly small weapons, rifles, pistols, and a small collection of other weaponry that wasn't particularly effective, and in many cases looked homemade. But it did include things like small artillery pieces. We were aware of a small, of a limited number of those that the Croatians had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say small artillery pieces, what are you referring to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I'm referring to the calibre of the weapons and their capability --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Such as? What type of weapon are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We're talking about -- I suppose to a nonexpert we're talking about cannon-type guns, guns that are mounted on wheels and can be moved around. And depending on their calibre and their power and the type of shells that they can fire is how effective they are. These were of the smaller variety, nothing like the size of the weapons we could see on the opposing mountaintops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means which mountaintop?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Which means Zarkovica and the areas that the shelling was coming from outside of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the state of Croatian ammunition resupply? What was the situation with the ammunition for the Croatian forces, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I can only say what I saw and what I was told. In both cases, I was told they were extremely short on ammunition. They were having great problems getting ammunition through the blockade, the naval blockade. They couldn't get anything overland. They were shipping it in where they could on speedboats at night and they were running into the blockade, and in many cases not being able to get through. When we went to positions like the position on the top of Mount Srdj, we were being told they had so little ammunition that they were under orders only to use it in extreme circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would that mean?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Basically when they were fired on, but even then only when they thought it could be effective. There was a policy, we were told -- my awareness comes only from what I was told. But there was a policy of only firing when they were fired upon, in order not to provoke an attack from opposition that was so much superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you discuss an attack on the 9th of November. And I'd like to try to get an idea of how that attack took place. First of all, was the Old Town implicated in the attack?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The Old Town -- I don't believe the Old Town was implicated on the 9th. I think that it was the 10th that we became aware of mortars falling into the Old Town and investigated that. If my memory serves me well, the 9th was when the much greater attack on Dubrovnik started and it involved bombing, planes bombing, warships appearing off the coast and shelling and using what appeared to be smaller guns. And some of the boats that I would characterise more as gunboats than warships. And the artillery firing from Zarkovica and other areas that we couldn't see. I'm not sure if on that day the Old Town was struck, certainly not as badly as it was later when we became more aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You make reference to a village called Bosanka. Do you have any recollection of its significance or its location in relation to Srdj or Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I believe it's somewhere beneath the two, if not directly in between the two, in that sort of area. It was in the disputed area, the area from which we would often hear gunfire at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took that position?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The JNA took it. At the time we arrived, it was still held by the Croatians. The JNA took it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your description of the greater attack, did that effect areas immediately surrounding the Old City of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these areas which contained a civilian population?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: They were, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going into your discussion about the 10th of November and the Old Town, describe, please, how you first found about the shelling. Where were you in the Old Town when it was shelled on that date?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We were filming somewhere other than the Old Town. We had a number of other vantage positions that gave views of other parts of Dubrovnik, and we had been touring the town as best we could in the circumstances to try and get a range of pictures of what was happening and also to see at times the attack would be concentrated on parts of Dubrovnik and very little on other parts. And we were basically just trying to find out where that was under attack and following the sound of noise and impact explosions to try and work out exactly who and what was on the receiving end. During the time that we were doing that, and we had been around the port area, we had been to a degree sort of at the side of Srdj to one of the roads that gave you a good view of some of the more modern parts of the city, while we were doing that, we became aware, we were told - I can't remember who by, there were newspaper journalists there as well, but also there were a number of Croatians around who would give you bits of information that was sometimes was rumour and sometimes turned out to be factually correct - but we heard that the Old Town had been hit, and at that stage that was still very, very unusual. We had been there quite a period of time by then, and we were starting to get into the mindset that the Old Town would be spared. So when we heard that it had been hit, we made our way there to investigate. While we were there, we heard an explosion of what we believed was a mortar in the Old Town. But we were told that there had been three others before we got there. And we were shown the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of any damage to any culturally valuable institutions in the Old Town on that date?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We were told and then we were shown damage at the Franciscan complex, of which there is a monastery there. And there's also, I don't know whether they actually call it a convent, but part of it there are monks and part of it there are nuns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 11th of November, does that date have any significance to you, other than that you were in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It has huge significance in that it was the day that everything really went -- seemed to go a bit crazy, and went up several gears in terms of the attack. It also has a personal significance; November the 11th is my birthday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in terms of the Old Town, that you recollect, on the 11th of November?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: On November the 11th, the Old Town was hit and it's my belief - and I'm as sure as I can be - that on that occasion it wasn't just from land that it was hit, but it was also from the sea because I saw ships firing and then, it was very close to an impact on the walls of the Old Town. But what was happening on that day was a much, much bigger attack on various parts of Dubrovnik. And a lot of it was falling -- a lot of the shells were falling very, very close to the Old Town inasmuch as we found a filming position on the ramparts near one of the gates. And we were able to film first the shells being fired from Zarkovica, and then to virtually follow their trajectory and then certainly follow the noise of it, and film the impact. They were falling just over our heads, over the walls of the Old Town and destroying buildings alongside the Old Town. And it was at that time, after quite a long period, hours, of watching, filming damage to these areas alongside the Old Town that we became aware that the Old Town itself was hit. And that's when I observed the ships firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a bit more detail I would like to get about what happened that day, but you made reference to some kind of trajectory, and I guess you're suggesting the recognition of projectiles. You described in your statement a pop. What is it that you were trying to indicate? Was there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. some sequence that became apparent?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes. It's very unusual. When you work trying to illustrate, trying to get pictures of what's happening in a conflict like this, one of the most difficult things to actually film is the point of shells, mortars being fired, and particularly the point of impact. Normally, when you look at war footage on television or the cinema, you see plumes of smoke and lots of damage and casualties. It's quite rare to actually hear and see the point of impact because the cameraman can only film when he sees that. On this particular day, and I was with a very, very experienced war cameraman, the shelling was so heavy and so consistent, we were able to recognise a pattern of noise followed by the trajectory of the shell and the point of impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that pattern? Can you describe it for us?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We would be standing on the walls looking and filming towards Zarkovica. We would hear -- it was like a pop noise, slightly muffled, coming from quite a distance away and obviously because it was from a distance away, you weren't hearing the exact moment it was fired. You were then able to, having heard that pop noise, you began to recognise how many seconds it would take before that shell, because it became quite apparent that that shell was being fired directly at us, albeit a few feet over our heads, they were falling. Where they were coming from was much higher than where we were. So they were coming down and then over our heads. So you recognised the pop noise. A number of seconds before the shell would arrive, you were able to turn the camera on, hear the whistle of the shell as it went over your head, and actually have the camera pointed at the place that you knew or believed that the shell was going the impact. And it happened over and over again. It meant that you were actually able to have the camera trained on a building and watch it's roof actually take the impact of the shell and the shell go through the roof and then the big explosion when it hit cars and other civilian areas. You were able to do the same. It's very unusual. I've never done it, seen it, or experienced it before or since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were able to hear the pop and then subsequently observe the impact, would it be fair to say that others around you would also have the same perception?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: They would. They would. They would. I would have to say that most of them would be in the shelters, but they would. And there's a very sinister whistling noise as the -- if you're anywhere near where the shells are being aimed at, a very sinister whistling noise as it comes in and then a few seconds of silence before the impact and then you wait. Because even when you're as experienced as we were and had seen lots of these shells by now going safely over your head and landing a bit further down, you didn't know it was definitely going to happen every time and that was always the worst time. And when you -- occasionally, we would be filming in shelters when people -- when the bombardment was happening overhead. That, for people, was always the time when you could see on their faces that they were terrified, having heard the original bang, and then waiting for that whistle and then the silence, and wondering where it was going to -- where the explosion was going to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were on the ramparts and were able to observe, did you at any time see any Croatian forces on those ramparts with any weaponry?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No, not at all. And I was looking for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just turning back perhaps a day or so. The use of helicopters, was there a use made by either side of helicopters that you could observe during this time period, during these days?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I believe there was. And again, some of what I say is just based on my own interpretation of what I saw. But at times of shelling, I would see JNA helicopters up in positions where they were safely out of range of anything that could be fired at them from the ground. But in positions where they could see what the effect of the shelling was, where the shells were falling, what damage was being caused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever observe any type of weapon that would be considered wire guided?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I did. And that was on the 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of weapon is it? Can you describe it, what its effect is, and from which forces it emanated.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: To describe it, it's a missile that has a length of wire behind it. In that sense, it's very easy to -- you don't have to be an expert to recognise a wire-guided missile. We were not in a position to see who had fired it, or indeed, it being fired, but we could see quite clearly where it was coming from. And it was coming from the area that was held by the JNA and it was being fired across the water in front of the hotels and the Hotel Argentina, which is where I was when I witnessed this, at the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe impacts of this wire-guided projectiles in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I observed and filmed dozens of impacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described a number of types of weaponry and approaches by the forces under the control of the JNA. Did you have any observation about any aspect of coordination, did anything occur to you about elements of coordination with regard to these various forces and the various types of weaponry used?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Only inasmuch as after a period of time you began to feel patterns, what was the norm and what wasn't the norm. And we became aware over this particular period of the 9th to the 12th of November that the whole thing had escalated and ratcheted up a notch or seven. Before there would be periods of shelling, there would be occasions when planes would appear and bomb certain targets and then it would stop and you didn't know when it was going to restart. There would be periods during the night where there would be fighting, and again it would go sometimes for three or four hours. But it would stop and then there would be long periods when it didn't. When we came to this particular period, starting on the 9th, that changed. We became aware that the artillery was firing from various places, including Zarkovica which we would see, that ships had appeared off the coast and were firing for long periods of time, that the planes were still coming and bombing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are from JNA --

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: These are all JNA forces. It was all happening at the same time and on a scale that we hadn't seen before. At the time in the report that I filed, I called it a coordinated attack and the first time that we had seen a coordinated attack involving land, sea, and air. And by that, I simply meant that for the first time we were seeing land, sea, and air forces used together and in a way and on a scale that we hadn't seen before. That was a complete change from what we had been witnessing before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you have described up to now the Croatian forces appear to have been land forces; would that be correct? Any Croatian defence was land-based?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I saw no air defences. And the only sea, if you would like to call them defences, that I saw were high-pass speedboats that were not fitted with any guns but were used for trying to run the blockade, to take out the wounded people and bring in ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had visited Srdj. Is there any particular feature of religious significance up on Srdj?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: There is a very large stone cross on the top of Srdj. I don't know it's full significance, but I do know that it seemed to become a target, particularly at this period of 9th to 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe anything about it on the 10th of November? Did something happen to that cross?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We had seen -- Even earlier than that, we had seen shells landing around it in a way that suggested to a layman that it wasn't a coincidence that they were so close to it. On the 10th, we actually saw it being hit, and later on, although I didn't witness and film it, it was hit a number of times. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen to you personally on the 11th of November?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I was caught by one of the -- in the blast of one of the shells that was fired. I believe this one came from the sea, I believe. And I was blown off my feet and had a piece of shrapnel embedded in my back. Not a very large piece and it didn't do any permanent damage. I was also unable to -- my hearing disappeared for a short time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you were injured?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Again, I was on the ramparts. It was at a time of very heavy shelling, and it was on one of the occasions that we were filming in particular the shelling from Zarkovica that was falling around the Old Town. I became aware as we were doing that that there was an explosion actually on the ramparts relatively close to where I was. It was still unusual enough, the Old Town being hit, to warrant investigation. And I went around to see if it had done any damage or whether it had just hit the outside of the old walls. And it was while I was looking to see what that first impact had done that I had a loud whistling noise and was caught by a second impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have referred to what has been characterised as a deliberately sustained assault against the Old City and the Old Town on the 12th of November. Would you please tell us why you have characterised it that way.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Because -- well, because it was clearly deliberate and it was certainly sustained. It went on for many hours. It seemed to be a culmination of what had been -- what we had seen on previous days. And on the 12th for the first time we saw the attack actually being concentrated or the greater part of the attack being concentrated on the Old Town. Even during the earlier days and quite possibly the 11th was the day when the most shells fell on Dubrovnik, but even during that time, there'd been a relatively small number of shells actually falling in the Old Town. The 12th was the day that we could see that the Old Town was now the target, and that was the day we saw the wire-guided missiles being fired again and again and again at the Old Town, hitting its walls and going into the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, based on your having been there, did you see any justification, provocation for that type of sustained, deliberate attack?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The European Community Monitoring Mission, we'll call them ECMM, did you observe that they were able to do anything to alleviate the situation, or what was your impression of their ability to actually intervene under these conditions?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: They were ineffective. They wanted to. They had neither the leverage nor the ability to make a significant difference. Earlier, they had been involved in attempting to negotiate cease-fires that we were aware of. And they hadn't come to anything. And I know that they were, from talking to them socially - staying in the same hotel - I know they were deeply frustrated by the situation that they were in, because most of the time all they could actually do is count the shells. And a lot of their jobs in the end came down to just making a record of what was happening, as opposed to being able to influence it. Certainly as the attack on Dubrovnik intensified, there was less and less that they felt they could do to the point where they were for periods of time, long periods of time, effectively trapped in the hotel, and whether deliberately or not, becoming targets themselves with shells hitting the Argentina hotel where they were based and having to take cover in safer parts of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Targeted by whose forces?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Again by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a perception among the civilian population, if you know, in Dubrovnik that there was some form of safety offered by this mission?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: There was certainly a hope that as long as the mission was there that it afforded some safety. There was also a belief that things that they'd heard about happening in other parts of former Yugoslavia wouldn't happen there and wouldn't happen to them as long as there were international observers in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The wire-guided missiles on the 12th of November, do you have any estimate of how many you may have observed? Did you attempt to keep any type of mental record?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. We filmed 15 impacts, 16, 17 impacts. We used more than half of those in the report that we used. We started filming sometime after the use of the wire-guided missiles had started. And it was still going on when we had moved on to film other things. My personal belief from what I saw was that dozens were used, not three figures, but certainly not 10 or 20 or even 30. Some were between 30 and three figures, but that is a very rough estimate. I certainly didn't count them, and they weren't the only thing that was happening at the time, so they weren't the only thing we were concentrating on. Having watched them for an hour or so, there were other things to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these wire-guided missiles were used exclusively by the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I certainly didn't see anybody else using them and at no time did we see any evidence that anybody other than the JNA had them. And we hadn't seen them being used before that day by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on what areas were impacted upon in the Old Town when you did your filming?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Well, from the time that the use of the wire-guided missiles started, it was the -- they were coming in from the south of Dubrovnik and either hitting or passing over the area of the Old Town where there was a little port, protected port area. They were hitting the walls of the Old Town. They were hitting the boats that were moored in the sheltered area, and some of them were passing over the walls of the Old Town. And there were explosions inside the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any observation as to whether or not any water craft may have been affected?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I mean, our film showed the moment of impact when a number of boats were hit and exploded and set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: A number of cars, the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The activity on the 12th from the JNA, it was not exclusively then wire-guided. Were there also -- did you observe other either artillery or other forms of infantry weaponry, like mortars, used?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We were aware of artillery being used, but our concentration was on the wire-guided missiles because we hadn't seen anything like it before, but those weren't the only explosions we were hearing that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on what, if any, response may have come from the Croatian forces from this what you call sustained attack by the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: During the time of the sustained attack, the Croatians fired back using the weaponry that they had. The only qualification I would put on that is that I don't believe it was from the Old Town, but they were using the weaponry that they had. And as I said earlier, I saw small artillery pieces and I saw mortars on the back of lorries being moved around. And there were clear attempts by the Croatians to get those pieces as close as they possibly could to what was firing against them. In many cases that was impossible, because planes and ships were well out of range. But there were a number of attempts to hit the artillery positions, particularly on Zarkovica. And on one of the days we filmed -- on a number of days we filmed unsuccessful attempts to do that with Croatian mortars landing short of the JNA positions. But on one particular day we filmed a, for the Croatians, a successful strike where they hit the position on the top of Zarkovica, and there was what we interpreted as being a series of secondary explosions that we interpreted as being an ammunition dump or something like that was detonated, because there was one main attack followed by a whole series of smaller explosions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to say there was no outgoing responsive fire - excuse me - coming from the Old Town that you observed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I am certainly able to say there was no outgoing fire from the Old Town that I observed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the attempts to get closer to the position at Zarkovica that you referred to, are you able to indicate that these attempts did not come from the Old Town, in other words they were outgoing fire, that these attempts also did not emanate from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I don't believe they came from the Old Town; I certainly didn't see them come from the Old Town. I was aware of attempts to -- clearly more than attempts to -- successful attempts to move mobile mortars into positions alongside the coast close to the Hotel Belvedere which was about the closest you could probably get to Zarkovica and still be in the Croatian-controlled territory. There was firing from there. We also heard on more than one occasion but were never able to film it, but were certainly aware that it happened, of the mortars being moved along the coast close to the Hotel Argentina. Again, it being one of the closest positions that you could get to the JNA position on top of the mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any effective Croatian response to the naval forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Not at all. That really wasn't possible, they were sitting so far out at sea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have provided a video of approximately 11 minutes. And I would ask for the exhibit number, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It has not been assigned a number. I'm sorry, I thought it was prenumbered. I will provide a copy of the transcript from that particular video clip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have spoken during the course of your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be Exhibit Number P19 and the transcript of the video, P19.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your testimony, you have discussed the filming of the attacks during the time period of 9 to 12 November. And what is in front of you is a transcript of a segment that is of the attacks. Have you previously reviewed, with the Office of the Prosecutor, the clip of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, do these attacks, first of all, represent the area of Dubrovnik that was the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: They do -- part of them do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: A part of them do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do they depict or do they show the Old Town during the time period of 9 to 12 November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the content of them reflect what you actually observed at the time that you were reporting for ITN?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It does. It's a concentrated view of them. They reflect, they're a sample of what happened over that -- a much longer period. For everything you see, that there were 10, 20, 30 others, but they are an example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there particular footage provided to your home office that was -- transferred up to your home office for publication?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it shown?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was shown. It was shown around the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I can please ask you to turn your attention to your monitors. We will be using the Sanction method of presentation, Your Honours, which is a software that actually has the video for you. And if there's any issue with its mechanical part, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any capacity to increase the sound?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We'll inquire with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The suggestion from the technical staff is that we might have our first morning break at this point whilst they pay some attention to the equipment in the hope of improving the sound. We will therefore break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the exhibit is now ready to be played.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, was it you who appeared in that video?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it you who narrated the video?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not -- I want to make sure I understood correctly, had the Chamber admitted this exhibit, P19 and P19.1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not need to further move for its admission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any opportunity after the shelling subsided to review the areas which were damaged in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes. On the following day, the 13th, we went into the Old Town briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your observations?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: A lot of damage, shell impacts. You could still see some of the missiles that hadn't exploded stuck in the walls of the Old Town, stuck in the areas of the harbour where they had fallen. You could see the damage from those that had exploded, both on the walls and on the roadways where they had landed and where they had landed on buildings causing damage and fires, where they had landed on cars that had been set on fire and destroyed. And most of the boats that had been moored in that little harbour in front of the Old Town had been set on fire and sunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your observation that the damage was concentrated in any particular area, or did you observe a dispersal of damage?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: There was a dispersal inasmuch as shells had fallen across the Old Town, really. But there was certainly a concentration of damage on that side, the south of the Old Town, from which the missiles were firing and where they had impacted against the walls and in some cases dropped over the walls into the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The missiles from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, or the position beneath Zarkovica where they were fired from but certainly from the direction of Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attempt to count the number of shells, that may have been more for your own information, but did you attempt to do so?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We did. Not during the time that the wire-guided missiles were being fired, but slightly earlier than that in the day. As an exercise we counted the explosions to try and get some sort of -- we were becoming aware that this was very, very heavy bombardment, more so than anything we'd experienced, and we just tried to gauge it in some way. And we counted the incoming explosions. We gave up -- we reached the number 1.000 and gave up on the exercise and returned to other things that we were doing. But we heard 100 -- sorry, I don't mean 100, I mean 1.000. We heard 1.000 explosions, and that's the point that we stopped counting. The explosions continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your video depicts a fair amount of impact with resultant fire. Can you comment on the capacity to extinguish the fire for the citizens of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Very difficult. Mostly because people weren't on the streets or in any position to do that; they were sheltering. At that time, the bombardment was so intense that nobody was on the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th -- was that -- that would be the day after the shelling?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The 13th was the day that we went into Dubrovnik Old Town and tried to get an idea of the damage that had been caused. The 11th was the day that we counted the 1.000 explosions and then gave up counting. And the 12th was the day when the Old Town took the most damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ECMM personnel were present and were shown in your video, did they remain in Dubrovnik very much beyond that, do you know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. They withdrew from Dubrovnik on the 14th. One of the reasons we were able to get some sort of a view on the 13th as to the damage that had been caused was because the -- after reaching the -- its heaviest level on the 11th and 12th, there appeared to be a cessation of shelling on the 13th, not total, but pretty much so, and we were informed that talks were taking place and one of the things those talks were involved in was negotiating some sort of a safe passage out of Dubrovnik for women, children, and other noncombatants that included the European Community monitors and most of the few remaining journalists who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason for the departure of ECMM, first part of the question; second part, was it expected; third part, how did the population view it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The reason was for their own safety. It wasn't expected. It was expected by them, and some of them expressed their disappointment at the decision to me. And the reaction of the population was one of almost impending doom. Basically there was a fear that this taking out of women, children, and anybody from outside who could witness what was going on was the prelude to something sinister that was about to happen. The feeling was that Dubrovnik was about to fall, and that only males and males of what's loosely termed "fighting age," were going to be left behind. And there was a terrible fear throughout Dubrovnik as to what was going to happen then. When the ferry that carried out the women and children and the ECMM monitors and others left, there were dreadful scenes on the dock side with women trying to get their teenage sons on to the boat. And in the end, police and armed men having to fight them back. The boat would only take a certain number of people; it was going to be checked by the federal military once it reached waters outside the port of Dubrovnik. And nobody beyond a certain age was going to be able to go beyond there. And there were dreadful scenes with people being forced back with rifle butts, because they were in a state of panic to try and get their kids out of there, fearing that any male that stayed behind wouldn't survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were in Dubrovnik, did Mount Srdj -- did Srdj ever come into the hands of the JNA or did it remain under the Croatian forces during your time there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I was never aware of it falling, but I was aware of a time when the bombardment of it was so intense that the Croatians withdrew from it. They went back up the next morning, had a rethink, and it hadn't actually been taken. But it was so bad that they did pull out. When the bombardment was at its heaviest and some of what you saw in the video there with shells falling, falling on it, hundreds of shells falling on it, there was no way you could survive staying on the outside, even the people who were supposed to be protecting it, defending it, withdrew into the cellars, and what have you, underneath it and took protection and waited for the bombardment to stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made reference to a demand by the JNA to the Croatians to surrender Srdj. Do you know what the response was by the Croatians to that demand?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I know they didn't surrender it. I do know on that occasion they pulled back, but that wasn't an official surrendering. That was just people deciding they weren't going to survive if they stayed there and briefly pulling out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any injuries that may have resulted from the shellings that you have depicted on your video during that time period? Was there an increase at all in the hospital capacity?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: There was an increase and we filmed on a number of occasions in the hospital. The hospital was full and people were being treated in areas other than the normal hospital beds. I was surprised that -- at the height of the bombardment that there weren't more casualties. But the civilian population appeared to be extremely diligent in taking to the underground shelters and staying in them for long, long periods of time. People were spending days in the underground shelters of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate that you had spent time yourself in a shelter?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it during a bombardment or was it just to experience the shelter itself?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people, if you're able to estimate, were in that shelter you found yourself in and where was that shelter?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The shelter I visited on at least two occasions was in the Old Town. It was close to the southern gates of the Old Town, and it was beneath the Old Town. You went down a number of old stone steps and into a cellar-like area that felt about as safe as anything was going to be. And on both occasions that I remember visiting it, there were people there, almost entirely civilians. And on the occasion that was during the bombardment, it was about as full as it could be. It's difficult to sort of put a figure on how many people were there, but I got the feeling that it was in three figures. I mean, it was more than 100. It -- I don't -- it wasn't several hundred. It was more than a hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present -- when did you actually leave Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I left on the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Across the Adriatic to Italy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return -- were you present in Dubrovnik for any activity on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was back in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may take a moment to consult. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were in Dubrovnik for, if perhaps any other means afterward, during the time you were there following these attacks, did you ever become aware of any either statement of concern, regret, apology, demand for investigation on the part of the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Not personally. Certainly during the time I was in Dubrovnik, I didn't hear anything like that, although the circumstances were very much a siege situation. We were not getting official sources of information. There were no press conferences or ministers briefings that you could go to to get information. An awful lot of what you found out was what you actually saw was happening and what you were able to glean from travelling around and talking to people. I was never aware of anybody apologising or saying it had all been a mistake. Later when I returned to London, I heard and saw various statements from Belgrade saying that the circumstances would be looked into. But that was months later and not anything I heard during any time that I was in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were not in Dubrovnik on the 6th of December, but were you still involved in covering the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I was. It was the conflict in a wider scale, the conflict in former Yugoslavia. It just happened to be one of the periods of time that I was at home between assignments in the former Yugoslavia. I received a phone call from some people in Dubrovnik telling me that they were coming under fire. They were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: On the 6th. They were under the impression, probably mistaken, but it was nice to hear that the report that we had managed to get out of the worst of the fighting in November, the attack on Dubrovnik seemed to stop or certainly be -- was brought down in scale when we managed to get those images out of Dubrovnik, which was very difficult to get out. And they reached the outside world. There appeared to be some sort of reaction to that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was after November?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That was after November and these people were calling and saying: "Help, we think you helped stop it last time, can you help again?" Which was very flattering, but completely unrealistic, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the shelling that you thought might come to an end in the November incident in fact saw -- was -- reared its head again on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Is it to be Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to be doing the cross-examination of this witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Davies, my name is Goran Rodic and I represent General Strugar. I'm going to be asking you a few questions on behalf of the Defence. On examination-in-chief you said that -- you gave us your CV. Is there anything you wish to add about yourself, and I mean do you have any special experience more important than the one that you mentioned during the examination-in-chief? So is there anything important in your CV that you didn't mention?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I've specialised in international news reporting for a number of years. And during those years, the world happened to be in a state that conflict was a large part of what was happening in the world. And that -- it turned into an area of speciality. I think I answered that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More specifically, did you report during the Gulf War? This is a well-known theatre of war. Were you there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I was. I was in the first, what they now call Gulf War 1, the first Gulf War. I was in Kuwait and in Iraq, and I was the -- what we call the pool correspondent. I was selected from the various news organisations in Britain to represent them all and be placed in the front line with the British troops during that conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that upon the invitation of the British Ministry of Defence that you reported for the Gulf War, or were you elected by the independent pool of journalists who delegated you to report on behalf of all of them?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was both. After negotiations between the greater body of all of the British news organisations and the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Defence agreed they would allow a very small number of reporters into various positions, on condition those reporters gave their work to everybody. There wasn't room to accommodate reporters from ITV, BBC, and the various newspapers. So one person was to be selected to represent and to report to all of the organisations. And once that had been agreed, then the news organisations selected the person who would fulfill that role. And there were a number of such people. One correspondent, well-known correspondent, Martin Bell from the BBC had one position with the British military, I had another in the front line with the army, another was on a warship, and another was with the RAF. But these people were selected from within the news organisations to fill roles that had been agreed between the news organisations and the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the selection of these journalists, did the Ministry of Defence play a decisive role when it came to the selection of the journalists who would report from the Gulf, and were these journalists official reporters affiliated with the British troops in the Gulf?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence did not play a decisive role in selecting the journalists. It laid down a few basic roles that covered fitness, but nothing beyond that. The journalists who were with the troops, if I can interpret what you mean by "affiliated," we lived with them. And as a condition of being with them, we wore the same clothes that they did. So in effect, we were in camouflage uniform. I mean, the simplest way of describing it is we were official war correspondents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to hear from you, because if you were official correspondents, then you obviously acted together with the British troops. And you yourself said you wore British camouflage uniforms. Am I right in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: In acting together with the British troops, yes, we travelled with them and, yes, we ate with them. We filmed what they were doing. We, however, controlled what we filmed and what we said in our reports. And at no time were the military able to dictate to us what we could -- what we were -- what we were to film or what we were to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how did you send your reports.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: They were sent from a satellite dish that was behind the front line. And we would send our pictures and my words, my commentary, narration, back to colleagues of ours, television -- British television colleagues of ours who were -- with this satellite dish who would put them together and they would be fed back to London and distributed to all of the news organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the satellite equipment, was that military equipment or was it your equipment, belonging to the journalists who worked in the area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
