utterances.text: It was our equipment. It was our satellite dish manned by our own engineers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the military have any influence on your report? Were your reports censored by the military, particularly the parts of your reports that referred to the troops and their activities during the war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The military did have influence on our reports, yes. In the first part they influenced them by -- we could -- our role was to report on what the troops were doing, where they were and what they were doing, as opposed to what was happening elsewhere. And therefore, the first influence was we could only do what they were doing and film what they were doing. We had as an organisation, and indeed the other news organisations, had independent teams that doing other things and independent teams on both sides of the front line and independent teams travelling between them. But our role was to film specifically with our own nation's forces and what they were doing. So that was one influence. And yes, there was an element of censorship. We were aware of it. It was a very simple form of censorship, so simple that in the most part you were -- you never fell foul of it because you knew the rules. You didn't say how many soldiers were with you. You could say what you were doing and the rough area where you were and what you had seen and show the images that you had filmed. You didn't say that there were 574 soldiers in the division. You didn't say exactly how many of each -- you could film the weapons they were using, but you didn't say exactly how many they had. You didn't say what they were going to do next. Those were all for strategic reasons, not because -- because with satellite television these days you wouldn't want to be giving anybody any immediate idea of what your next step was. And then there was another level of censorship which was that when you took casualties, you didn't film their faces or identify them before their families had been identified and all of the humane considerations that you would have towards the families of victims. So that was the form of the censorship. It didn't go beyond that and it didn't certainly cover any dictating what you were going to say. It just restricted some of the elements as I've detailed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind those limitations that you have just described, can you please tell us whether anybody together with you or without you on behalf of the military inspected your reports before they were dispatched to wherever they went?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I believe that there was a level of inspection. That was where our satellite dish was based, that basically checked that none of the details that I've just outlined had been broken or ignored. And then the report could be sent. It might be useful to say that this occasion that we're talking about now is the only occasion in my long career that I've worked within the constrictions of working within the military. Life is a lot simpler when you are an independent covering a conflict and able to view life from both sides and do exactly as you please, as was the case in Dubrovnik and has been the case in 99 per cent of the assignments that I've had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please be more precise and tell us who was it who checked your reports?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I can, yes. There were -- there was a British army colonel who was responsible for checking the reports before they were sent back out of the, what they call the theatre, the conflict area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you well? Did you say this was your first experience of the kind with regard to the reporting from a theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was the first experience of being, if you like, on the inside. Certainly in uniform being with a particular group of people and having to abide by certain restrictions. It was the first time and pretty much the last time that I experienced that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must ask you, since you've mentioned it yourself, comparing the experience from Dubrovnik with that experience, did you have an occasion in Dubrovnik to report from both sides, or were you pretty much involved only with one -- from one side, that is, the territory and the area from which you had the best view of the other side? So what kind of reporting was that from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: In Dubrovnik, I was only able to report from the inside, if you like, from the Croatian side. There are a number of reasons for that. The main is that I specifically set out to be on the inside of the siege. And having done so, it was not possible to swap sides from time to time. You were either in or out. My organisation, ITN, had on occasions teams on the JNA side operating out of Belgrade. But during the time of this particular assignment in Dubrovnik, I was on the inside of the situation in Dubrovnik and unable to reach the outside, had I so desired. And on occasions, I did so desire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of your reporting from Dubrovnik on the other side, so to say, on the side of the JNA, on the positions of the JNA, you did not have another colleague working for the ITN at the same time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I believe there was one occasion when a colleague was able -- coming from Belgrade was able to reach Zarkovica, but it wasn't for any longer than a brief visit. But certainly we carried one report from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any attempts by your colleagues to get to the JNA positions in order to report from those positions? Were there any such attempts that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes. We had a team based in Belgrade that was constantly trying to reach situations of conflict from the JNA side and on many occasions were able to do so. They would do it through the appropriate ministry in Belgrade. And I mentioned one visit to Dubrovnik that was arranged. But there were many successful assignments that were organised to places like Vukovar and elsewhere from the JNA side. It was a constant presence in Belgrade and constantly applying for permissions to get close to where things were happening, where it was impossible to reach merely as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why was there more or less interest on your behalf to reach the positions of the JNA around Dubrovnik; that is, were your colleagues from your TV station less interested in reaching those positions around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I don't think they were less interested in reaching. It's hard to answer for other people. I know that they were applying for permissions to do so, and on occasion they were being granted permissions to go to places of conflict. I don't know why a certain area was successfully visited and why others were more difficult. That's problems experienced by other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then have any real information coming from the other side; for example, about their casualties, about the fallen soldiers of the JNA, on the ceasefire that was broken by the Croatian side, about provocations from the Croatian side towards the JNA side? Did you have any such information at all?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Not really. The -- from the position that we were in -- and again, I would try and ask that it be appreciated that during a time of conflict, normal avenues of gaining information become quite difficult. But most of what I saw and therefore what I reported had to be, of necessity, an eyewitness account. And inasmuch as that it was based not in general terms of the greater situation between Belgrade and Zagreb or what was happening elsewhere in former Yugoslavia or even what was happening outside, immediately outside Dubrovnik, by necessity, my report was what I and my team saw and understood from our own experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how big the Dubrovnik area is, how big the Dubrovnik municipality is? How far does it extend towards the Montenegrin border, how far does it extend to the Bosnia-Herzegovinian border? Do you know how big that area is, if you know, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that and I certainly wouldn't want to guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you then at least aware of the fact that the area of the municipality of Dubrovnik and the zone of activities during the year 1991 was elongated because of the configuration of the terrain and the shape of the town and the municipality that extended along the coastline?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say that I was aware of what was happening within the area that I was able to travel in, and I wasn't aware of what was happening elsewhere and therefore didn't offer any opinions or reports of what was happening outside of my knowledge and what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area that we are discussing, which is Dubrovnik, and let me ask you more specifically, are you familiar with Rijeka Dubrovacka, the Gruz harbour, Babin Kuk on the one hand, and on the other hand towards the Cilipi airport, are you familiar with that area? This is all the territory of Dubrovnik municipality, and also this was all within the zone of combat activities. So are you familiar with the entire area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the entire area or I certainly wasn't familiar with the entire area at the time. I knew the port area, as you describe, and I knew the area, obviously, around the Old Town. And beyond the Hotel Belvedere was impossible to travel. So I had and my team had no information as to what was happening towards the airport area. There were occasions later in my assignment when with the help of ceasefires we were able to travel to places like Mokosica and other areas that had fallen to the JNA. But during the main part of the time I spent in Dubrovnik, we were restricted to the areas that were still held by the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Lapad?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to Lapad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and where exactly did you go?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I -- it's difficult to answer that. I went there one night when there was a shelling and the shelling was still going on and buildings were on fire. And my team filmed that and people evacuating their houses. And then we withdrew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a report on that visit to Lapad? Did you report it on your visit?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever broadcast that report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, as part of a larger report, but yes, it has been broadcast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to your stay in Dubrovnik, would you be able to pinpoint the period when you went to Lapad?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I believe it was in the early part of the stay. I couldn't give you an exact date, but it was in the period between the 31st, when I arrived, and the 4th or 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you base this on what?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Well, I base what I'm telling you on my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also base everything you told us earlier today on your memory when you mentioned all the dates? Did you also base that on your memory?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. Obviously partly my memory, but also I have had the opportunity of reading some of the things that I wrote at the time, knowing that I was coming here, and also viewing some of the reports that I compiled at the time, again knowing I was coming here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have those notes? Are they in your possession? Are these just written reports or are we also talking about video footage of some events? And another thing I would like to ask you: If the things that you used to refresh your memory, are they something we did not see on the video footage that we saw today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The principle thing that refreshed my memory was the footage that you saw today. There would have been some other footage that I've looked at as well that you haven't seen today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the investigators of this Tribunal ever have an opportunity to see your notes and this video footage, did you ever show those to them? And is this film that they showed us today the result of a selection process? Did they have an opportunity to select from all our notes and all the video footage that you have?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I don't believe that there was a selection process, in that I don't think other footage that I've mentioned was even available to them. Certainly they haven't seen any notes. There was -- one of the other films that would have refreshed my memory was the film of the journey into Dubrovnik, and I don't know whether the investigators here would have had access to that. But I think it was used as part of a previous trial, so maybe they would have access to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report that you mentioned that covered your visit to Lapad and the shelling that took place that night, is it true that this report is not part of the footage that we saw earlier today in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how many such video reports do you still have and also, if you have them, is it true that they go beyond of what we saw today in the courtroom, so they do not cover the same things?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: There were approximately, and this is not an exact number at all, there were approximately five or six reports broadcast from Dubrovnik or smuggled out of Dubrovnik prior to the main report, the large report, that you have seen today. And I think there were probably three or four reports after the report that you've seen today. I didn't leave Dubrovnik until the 21st of November, and we were still sending reports up until the time that we left. The report that you have seen today is the report that covers the main attack, and the -- what turned out to be the four days of heaviest fighting. There were other reports, both before it and after it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in addition to this big report that covers the days with the heaviest shelling, am I right in thinking there are six or seven other reports in addition to that comprehensive one?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Some of them in the early days showing rationing and people with shortages of water and power and others that show as the fighting became -- or the shelling started, the earlier damage, building up to the one that you've seen today. The significance of the one you've seen today is that at the time, first of all, that it covers the period of the heaviest fighting; and secondly, that it covers a period of time where we couldn't get our reports out of Dubrovnik, and therefore we used the material we had to in effect make a diary of what turned out to be the four days of heaviest fighting. Up until then, we had been able to get out stories on any given day that were a minute long, a minute and a half long, much shorter than this one, just covering what was happening on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you make the rest of your reports from Dubrovnik available to the Defence? We would very much like to look at those reports.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I personally wouldn't be able to make them available, but it would be a request from yourselves to my company, which I think is the course that the Prosecution would have taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you earlier whether the Prosecution had received those other reports and whether they had an opportunity to look at them.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: They certainly haven't received them. And I don't think that they have even been able to see them. I think that it's -- it might be quite telling, the fact that even the version that we have seen today, the quality isn't wonderful. And it doesn't look to me like something that a broadcast company has made available. It almost looks like it's something that's been recorded off air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all these reports, including the one that we saw today, did you include the coverage of the Croatian positions, the Croatian artillery, the actions of the Croatian artillery? Is there anything else in addition to your visit to Srdj, which we didn't see in the footage that we saw earlier today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: There would have been some other things, illustrations of the Croatians' weaponry, but not a great deal, as partly they didn't have a great deal of weaponry and partly the way that it was used made it almost impossible to capture it in action. We on a number of occasions, and some of them are in the footage you have seen, filmed Croatian mortars being fired at JNA positions. We were never in a position to film the mortars being fired, although on occasions I saw them, witnessed with my eyes being moved between different firing positions. The nature of the defence was that they had very, very few weapons, and what they did have were not particularly powerful --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. Let me interrupt you for a moment. We are going to come to that later on, but since -- from the qualifications that were mentioned at the beginning of your examination-in-chief, I got the impression that you are a very experienced journalist, that you covered very specific areas, that you are an official war correspondent, that you have been through various theatres of war. And correct me if I'm mistaken, I would assume that for you, an action or a movement of one or the other side would constitute the most important and the most interesting thing. It would be very interesting for you to film such a movement or such an action in order to show it in your report. Am I right in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: You are right in assuming it and you would be right in assuming that we attempted on many occasions to film both sides of even what was a very one-sided conflict. We were very keen to show that -- and in fact, if you remember from the words I used in my main report, I make the point that it may have been one-sided, but both sides were involved in it and firing at each other. We tried as best we could to illustrate what the Croatians were doing, and it was very difficult. They were constantly on the move and very keen, as much for their own lives as anything else, not to be witnessed and not to be in any one place for very long. Effectively they had two or three mortars on the back of the lorry. They moved it as quickly and quietly as they could to a position where they thought they might be able to target the opposition guns. They fired their mortars and then they moved on so as not to be hit. It made them very, very difficult to film in action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were answering the questions put to you by my learned friend, you mentioned having seen the movement of Croatian mortars along the coast between the hotels Belvedere and Argentina. If you noticed that, could you please specify the distance and also can you tell us whether you filmed that movement, whether you filmed that action; if not, why didn't you do that, why didn't you film that movement between those two hotels?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Sure. Well, you're not quite right. You've mixed up two things. Yes, I did see the movement with my eyes in the Dubrovnik area of Croatian mortars. And yes, I know that mortars were used to fire at the JNA from between the hotels Belvedere and Argentina, but they're not the same event. I saw the mortars in the -- not in the Old Town, but in areas of the New Town being moved, and I heard on two or three occasions, very loudly, the mortars being fired from between those hotels, Belvedere and Argentina. And on the occasions we heard them being fired, we took our equipment and tried to get to a position where we could film them, not easy as that's where you are in line of fire from the people that were on Zarkovica. But also they were moving on, so we didn't film them. But I can quite truthfully say, yes, they had mortars and, yes, they fired them from those areas. What I'm not able to give you is the images of them because we weren't able to capture those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you well that because of the tactic that they employed, the crews of the Croatian mortars, it was very risky to film a situation like that because of the way they moved and because of the way they engaged in action?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes. You are right in understanding that. That wouldn't have stopped us filming if --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we are talking about this kind of tactic employed by the Croatian artillery, is it because of that tactic that you were in a position to see a speedy response by the JNA artillery towards the place from which the Croatian artillery had fired, and was that one of the risks involved in filming such a situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I object, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise from the interruption, however I know that the Chamber has distinguished between leading questions on cross and testifying by counsel, and I suggest what we just heard is testimony by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I did not detect that at the moment. It seemed to me that there was a very lengthy question which involved more than one proposition being put to the witness. I'm not sure yet how Mr. Davies will be able to cope with it and react to it. If it had been broken up into smaller elements, it would have been more manageable. So we'll see how the witness copes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not easy to see what you're getting at from that. Perhaps it would be better if it was individual questions. If what you're trying to get at is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On several occasions, you mentioned the tactics used by the crews of Croatian mortars. They would fire and then immediately leave the place from which they had fired to go on to the next place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the most frequent manner in which you noticed that Croatian mortars fired while you were in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Certainly that seemed to be the tactic that they were using most of the time, yes. They never stayed in one place very long for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these obvious reasons were.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That the mortars that were being used were a very, very small number of weapons. And they were in line of fire of a far superior number of heavier weapons. And by opening fire themselves, they gave their position away and invited a response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you were able to see the JNA response to the fire from Croatian mortars?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I was able to see the JNA firing, both firing in response to Croatian mortars and firing when apparently not in response to anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you certainly had occasion to observe the JNA firing in response to previous fire by Croatian artillery, or rather, the mortar crews?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't characterise it like that. I certainly saw the Croatian artillery or mortar crews firing, and I certainly saw them moving to avoid a response. I couldn't put my hand on my heart and say that one side had started today's firing or the other side had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But specifically when you say you saw them firing and then moving on, not waiting for a response, were you able to observe that the JNA was responding to that fire by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I was certainly able to observe that the firing that had already started prior to -- prior to even me being aware of what or who was firing was continuing and that it was continuing from the JNA positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct then that you were often unable to discern who had actually started the shooting, bearing in mind of course the size of the entire area of Dubrovnik municipality, which I asked you about before, and the disposition of the JNA forces and the Croatian forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It's certainly correct to say that there were very few occasions that anyone, barring a commander who had given an order, would be able to stay in an area that large who had fired what shot first. What you could clearly see was the scale of what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if this is a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is in matter of time. I thought you were into an area of great interest, so I was delaying. But we'll break now, Mr. Rodic. The break will be for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, let's go back to the video footage that we've seen today. You've told us that you used notes and video footage that you made before coming here to this Tribunal in order to refresh your memory of the events that took place in 1991, bearing in mind the lapse of time. Bearing that in mind, I would like to know, since I didn't notice on the footage that there was any date on the footage. And while you were talking about the footage, you said that it was recorded over a period of several days. I would be interested to know how could you tell when the events took place, being aware of the fact that there are no markings on the video footage that would place the events in certain periods of time.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Right. That's actually quite easy. Each part of the report that you saw was actually put together in the evening of the day that it took place. And as the period of time went on, the report grew. We didn't know how long its ultimate length was going to be; it turned out to be four days. As far as being sure at what time the original footage had been filmed, although there is no marking on the image that you see, the actual tape and the box that it goes into both have all the detail of dates, times, and locations. And also, of course when you're putting together, it's very much in the forefront of your memory, having happened in the hours before. The images you saw, the report you saw there was all completed by the evening of the 12th of November. Nothing was added after that. When the final edit was completed on the evening of the 12th of November, many copies of it were made and attempts made to get them out of Dubrovnik by various ways. The -- one of the ways obviously worked and it was sent back to London and then passed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just told us that everything was filmed before the 12th of November and that everything was edited on the evening of the day and that everything was filmed by the 12th of November. At the beginning it was said that this film covered only a four-day period, the 9th, the 10th, the 11th, the 12th of November. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how do you remember what was going on before these dates, before the 9th of November?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I remember from my memory, and since 1991 I have viewed the earlier reports that we sent on more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the only trace that you have should be found on the box where this film is stored, the film that you recorded on the 9th, 10th, 11th, and 12th of November. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It's not the only place that you would find evidence of what happened that day. The most important source would be the narration which was actually written and put on to tape on the very day that it happened. And there is no better source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to this film, did you also hand over to the investigators anything else, the box or some notes that would serve to identify the events depicted in this film? As we have already said, there are no markings of the events on the images itself.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No, I did not hand over anything else that would have served to identify the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have also noticed that the timing on the film, that is, the time in the corner, does not start with a zero. Can you explain that. Is that part of a whole, of a bigger film, or has this film been compiled from a number of other films? What is it all about?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The film that you have seen is as it was originally compiled, but the -- they seem to have clipped both the start and the end of it, nothing more than that as far as I can see. It's just slightly sloppy, in that it's not -- there are a few seconds missing at both ends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who did that, who is it that clipped the beginning and the end of the film?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I don't know. They haven't missed anything significant, as far as I can see, but no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how did the OTP get hold of this video footage? Was it you who handed it over or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell us who?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't you be interested in finding out who is it who handed over this film that you yourself, as you've told us, recorded while you worked in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Only a little. As I said earlier, this report, as it was the only visual report of what was happening in Dubrovnik, was immediately shown around the world after it was smuggled out of Dubrovnik. Copies of it will exist in the libraries of almost every major news organisation. I myself have seen it popping up in various places around the world since it's something that happens when you have a very exclusive piece of news footage. Suddenly it becomes world property and it crops up everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this footage is exclusive. You've seen it popping up all over the place. Is this the version identical to the one that we've seen today here, or maybe those versions that you've seen elsewhere contain other things, particularly a bit more at the beginning, a bit more at the end?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. The versions that I've -- that I've seen are the same as the version today. When I say a few seconds are missing, that's all it is. Possibly the last image you saw has been cut short by two or three seconds, and obviously the same has happened at the top. But we're not talking about anything of any substance missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 12 years, how can you remember that it is only a couple seconds missing at the beginning and a couple seconds at the end, and that there is nothing significant happening during those couple of seconds missing at both ends? How can you remember after such a long time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I would know if there was something important missing or if it had been in any way altered or messed about. I would know. It's an important piece of my work and even after all these years, it's still a piece that I remember very well, and I would know if somebody had been trying to alter it in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, you yourself have noted those parts missing. You've said that only a couple of seconds are missing, but that may be even a couple of minutes. What I would like to state is that we are not talking about the film that you made, that it has been altered. And also I would like to say that you have used it to identify the events depicted on the movie, and that you also used the data recorded on the box of the film. Since you were not the one who handed over the movie, how could you then recall the events on the movie, reading the data recorded on the box?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Well, for a start, I have also seen the original copies of this film, which allows me to know what it was like in its original form, and that that form is all but the few seconds that we are discussing, the form that you have witnessed. I think that maybe we're making, or rather, with respect, you're making a little bit too much about these seconds that are missing. When I pick them out, I'm talking maybe a little bit as a professional in the business when I see something that has a messy start, even if it's only missing a second or two, it offends me. And the same at the end, where it's clipped. This is my work; it's not been presented very well, so I don't like to see it like that so maybe I pick that out. You're missing nothing more than what you have already started to see and then there's a second or two that has been clipped. It is nothing sinister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate your view of a professional who authored this work, and I understand if you're offended if somebody tampers with your work and if somebody makes a decision of what is going to be clipped from the movie. Would you then be able to tell us who it is who did that, why this was done? What was the reason to do it? It is your professionalism that would naturally make you curious to find out who it was who decided to do that.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Again, I would only say that so little is lost that we're effectively just talking about presentation. And it looks a bit messy to enter something a second late or two late. And it looks messy to finish it a second late or two late. It's the sort of thing that happens quite frequently when a news bulletin is running and somebody has what we call finger trouble and they bring up the report while the newscaster is still saying here's the report. And you miss the first second or maybe they come out of it one second early. It's just something that happens and it really isn't anything serious in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the technicians to show us just the beginning of the video footage, the Exhibit Number 19 that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can stop it here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the video footage, 0 should be hours, 35 should be minutes, and 32 should be seconds. According to this, it seems that we are in the 35th minute of the film, rather than the first couple of seconds missing.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It's -- I can't tell you for sure. I can offer an opinion. The opinion would be that the number which is imposed on the top of the screen has absolutely nothing to do with the report that you're seeing. It certainly wouldn't have been on there when we put the piece together. It wasn't there when we put it together, and it wouldn't have been there when it was broadcast. It appears to me that that number has come from wherever the -- this material was being transferred on to the format, on to the tape, that it is now on, and that those numbers relate to what was happening on to -- on that particular tape that they were being recorded on. If I'm not making myself clear, what I'm trying to say is something along the lines of if you had a tape which had, say, 34 minutes worth of material on it already or 35 minutes of material on it already, and the next thing you wanted to put on to this tape way my report and you first left a little gap between the last thing and this starting, maybe that's why it's got 35 minutes up there. I can see no other explanation for it. It has nothing whatsoever -- that number that appears there has nothing whatsoever to do with this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help me with the abbreviation CDL, what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Again, I have no idea. This has come from some later stage long after this material was put together by myself and my team and broadcast. It's not something I recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you don't know what could be found on this tape in the first 35 minutes that are missing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: If this number refers to, and it quite possibly does, that -- the time, then I have no idea what was on that particular tape. It could be a tape that was in a studio anywhere and is 34 minutes worth of material. But I certainly wouldn't know the identity of it before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the technicians to fast forward this footage to about the middle. The total length of the video footage is 11 minutes. Can we have it around the fifth or the sixth minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's happening, Mr. Rodic, can I just make clear as the Chamber understands it, this material is not in the hands of the technicians of the Tribunal; it's in the hands of the Prosecution over there on their machine. And I'm sure that we will be assisted in due course by Ms. Somers with the provenance of this tape, which at the moment seems something of a mystery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe this would actually make my cross-examination shorter if we knew the source -- the provenance of this video footage. Maybe that would help me not waste everybody's precious time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a good idea, Mr. Rodic. Are you in a position to assist us, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we can have a few moments to see if we can call up the necessary material. If not, I may have to ask for a five-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Accessing to get information out of this particular computer system to get anything back. Would it be possible to return to this point. If we are unable to do this from here, I will ask my colleague to try to go upstairs and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, would it be possible for you to move on to some other areas with a view to this information being provided before you finish your cross-examination. And if there's then anything that requires further exploration by you, you could do it at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm ready to move on and address another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before your arrival in Dubrovnik, Mr. Davies, did you visit any other place in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes. Shortly prior to my -- the visit to Dubrovnik, I had been in Zagreb and other places outside, Vukovar, Vinkovci, Osijek, a number of other places, but areas where there were problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you departed for Dubrovnik on 28 or 29 October. Can you be more specific on the period of time that you spent in Croatia all together when you mentioned Zagreb and other places. How much time prior to your departure to Dubrovnik did you spend in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Three weeks. Three weeks, and it was a three-week period that ended I think on the 26th of October. Certainly I was only back in London for the very brief time before I set off for Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reporting mission during that three-week period in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was to see and to report on as much of the problems that were happening there as I was able to, and that involved areas where there was fighting, areas where there were disputes over JNA army barracks that were still in areas of Croatia like Zagreb where there were disputes over the weaponry that was in them and sieges taking place, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this fighting that you covered, who were the sides involved in it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The sides involved in it were Croatian military and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to report and to witness the blockades of JNA barracks, and if you did, where did you see that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I did witness that, and I witnessed it for the most part in -- near to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the situation in the former Yugoslavia once you arrived to report from Croatia in 1991? Were you familiar with the political situation with the social circumstances with what had been going on in that area prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I was aware in the broadest of terms. I knew about the breakaway of Croatia and other areas. And I knew of the conflicts that were resulting from that. I did not have an in-depth knowledge of the history of the region. It was, for me, the early stages of what was to be a very long assignment or series of assignments in the former Yugoslavia. It was back in the early days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the JNA a legal armed force of the former Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing your reporting experience, did you find such a situation unusual -- did you find it unusual to see that the barracks of the legal armed force were blocked?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was unusual, yes. But then again, we had already at that stage witnessed in Eastern Europe a whole series of unusual events with the forces that had been -- the legal forces being challenged, and in some cases overthrown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us something more about your departure for Dubrovnik. How did you gain an opportunity to travel to Dubrovnik? I believe that at the time you had had information that Dubrovnik was blocked. Did you have somebody who assisted you with going there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We didn't have any assistance in the planning of going to Dubrovnik. We set out hoping that it would be possible. I've set out on many assignments over the years where it's turned out to be impossible to reach somewhere that's under siege. We set out hoping we would be able to get through, and as we were travelling we learned that there was to be an attempt, a very high-profile attempt to break the blockade from a flotilla of boats that would be carrying artists, musicians, various artists, and indeed, some politicians, who were going to make a very public show of trying to get through the blockade in order to highlight the growing problems inside Dubrovnik. We heard about this attempt and we decided we would try to join it, if nothing else, even if it didn't succeed, it would give us our first story of the assignment. We travelled down the coast on a ferry from Rijeka. As we were travelling, we heard that this flotilla was actually setting out of Split, the port of Split. We made radio contact via the craft we were travelling on. And they agreed to delay their departure by a very short time in order to take a foreign film crew on board, and this is what happened. They stopped just outside the port of Split, and we were transferred from our craft to join the flotilla, which ultimately took us into Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you accredited? Did you have your credentials to report from Dubrovnik? How could you enter?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. They seemed to accept the fact that we were obviously, by the equipment we were carrying, a film crew. And we had our own press passes. But no, we had no Croatian accreditation, or indeed, any accreditation from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us please, when you boarded the Slavija ferry, how long did your journey on this ferry last before you reached the port of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The best part of two days the journey lasted. It included one night of travelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had an opportunity to meet the passengers on the ferry. You could also compile some sort of a report on that journey and the passengers that you had joined?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We interviewed some of the passengers. There were some people who, although not particularly well-known to us, we were told were very famous singers and artists in their own country. And we talked to them about why they were doing it, why they were taking the risk, what they hoped to achieve. And a good deal of the time was also spent in negotiating with the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll come back to that later. Do you remember any of the more prominent names or their positions, or do you remember what they represented in the cultural or artistic life of their country? Or maybe you remember some of the politicians who were on board?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: With regard to the artists, I don't remember their names. They were not people that I had known before. I do know that -- from the welcome they received in Dubrovnik, that they were extremely well-known in former Yugoslavia. I remember there was a well-known singer, a well-known painter; I don't remember their names. I do remember the name of the best-known politician who was on the flotilla, it was Stipe Mesic. He was on the Slavija ferry, the same ferry we were travelling on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what post he held as a politician at that time, what his position was, his office?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know what his post was at the time. I know he was a very senior politician, the most senior person on the flotilla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly in your estimation how many approximately were on board in the whole flotilla, if you have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I could only give you an opinion, 100, 200. It's very difficult to say. There were many, many small boats. And having said that, many of them only had two or three people on. There were fishing boats, there were even smaller boats. It would be very difficult to give an accurate number. Certainly the ferry Slavija was very full and we were sleeping on the deck. But that's -- by saying 100 to 200, that's as close as I can get, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility of there being more people in that flotilla?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I would doubt it, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about the kind of passengers. I'm interested in the ratio of men and women, for example.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I'm afraid, if I'm being honest, I must admit I really can't remember the breakup of men and women. There were both and I seemed to sense there were more men than women, but I can't be any more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there were about 200 passengers, were you told they were all artists?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Well, for the start when I say -- when we use the figure 200, and it's a very loose figure, it doesn't refer solely to the ferry, the Slavija. We weren't told who everyone was. We knew who some of them were. I wouldn't know who everyone was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I interrupted you a little while ago. I assume that the vessel was checked on its entry into Dubrovnik. Can you tell us who did that and why?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, I can certainly tell you that it happened and sailors people from what I would describe as the gunboats that had stopped the ferry came on board and searched the boat -- this was after some time. The ferry was stopped and there was a period of negotiation. The closest that we came to being briefed on what these negotiations were all about was very unofficial conversation. And that basically told us that, first of all, we had been stopped and they wanted us to turn back; and then that there was discussion going on about would we be allowed to continue, and if so under what conditions; and then ultimately we were searched. Sailors came on board, looked in the hold in particular. And eventually we were allowed to travel on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In brief, do you know who conducted the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I don't know who negotiated -- who conducted the negotiations, but I do know that certainly Stipe Mesic was in the control room of the Slavija at the time. We took pictures of him talking to somebody. Whether that was the negotiations or something that was going on alongside it, I don't know. But he was certainly there, and we took pictures of him at the time. I don't know who he was negotiating -- who he or anybody else that was negotiating was talking to. I mean, it was the military, and the military that was going to decide whether or not we could go on. But we didn't -- I didn't know who the person was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your arrival in Dubrovnik you said you were put up in the hotel Argentina. I would like to know about your movements through the town, about how you gathered information, were you aware of the information centre in Dubrovnik? Did you have contacts with them or someone else as regards your movement around Dubrovnik, and areas or events of interest for your work? Did you have any assistance in that direction and from whom?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I was aware of the information centre. And on occasions one would seek information or whatever from them, but they were not really very much use in the job we were trying to do. I mean, we didn't want a party line or propaganda or anything that we didn't -- couldn't necessarily believe. In the situation what we were in, what we really wanted to do was to travel around and see for ourselves what was happening and film it. In a situation like that, where you're only seeing one side of a conflict, the only meaningful reporting is your own eyewitness account, and that's what we were trying to achieve. In trying to do that, we took help from anybody that was able to give us information as to this is where there's a big problem or that's where there's a big problem. And eventually we managed to obtain vehicles of our own. But in the early stages, the early days, we were also begging and borrowing vehicles to allow us to travel to the different areas of Dubrovnik to film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As this was a war-affected area and you've just explained the problems in moving about, did you have any escort or any help by any of the locals or officials in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: At times, yes; and at times, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that was.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: At times, particularly in the early days before we got a good understanding of the layout and where everything was, there was a part-time policeman who helped us whenever we needed to get to any areas where we were likely to run into officialdom saying, "No, you can't come here".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this policeman in uniform and was he carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No. When he was with us, he wasn't in uniform or carrying weapons. But at other times of the day, like almost all of the males of that age, he did have a role in the defence of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was he?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I would say in his 30s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring to one person who was with you on more than one occasion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I am, yes. He was probably with us on 3 or 4 occasions. He was with us on one occasion where there was fighting at night-time and it required local knowledge to get to where it was happening. He also guided us the first time that we went up to search after those first couple of days, partly because he was doing other things and partly because we were finding our own way around and eventually got our own vehicles. We didn't see much of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you come to meet this policeman? Who did you apply to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: We didn't apply. We met him in the harbour on our arrival. He helped us transport some of our equipment to the Argentina hotel and asked if we needed him at any stage to -- as we were newly arrived, to give him a call and he would offer his advice and help where he could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that you also used him to go to a place where there was shelling at night, can you explain why? What was his role? Did he enable you to get to a place where you wouldn't be able to get to otherwise? Was it because of the positions of the Croatian army or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: In many cases, it was even simpler than that. We didn't know our way around at all, and certainly not at a time when there was fighting and shelling. And he had a vehicle and he was prepared to show us where this was happening and also to help us to get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me in your view what his motive was, why did he do this?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: I think his motive, principally, was that he was very pleased that a foreign television crew was present in Dubrovnik so the outside world would see what was happening. And he wanted to give us what assistance he could in making sure we could do our job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me very briefly, during your stay there were you ever given any kind of assistance by the Croatian army just -- well, in the same way that you received assistance from this policeman who you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: No, no. I mean, we received assistance inasmuch as they allowed us to film them sometimes when we went to try and talk to people, to interview people. But we were never taken by them to anything or what we would call a facility to see them in action or carrying out some sort of operation. There was no cooperation like that. In fact, we would have been looking for some form of organisation along those lines to try and get to certain places. And we didn't find that there was that degree of organisation. It seemed to be on a much, much less sophisticated level, which left us pretty much wandering around as best we could finding things for ourselves and coping for ourselves. Very unlike what I would later come across in former Yugoslavia where the operation in handling the press, and particularly television crews, became very, very sophisticated on all sides. This wasn't like that, but it was early days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned members of the Croatian army who allowed you to film them as you explained in a limited way, how did you come into contact with them and who did you come into contact with? Was it an ordinary private or a higher-ranking officer? Who did you apply to for such permission?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Generally, during the course of our travels on a particular day trying to see what was happening, we would come across something or somebody. And we would either, if the situation was appropriate, simply film them without asking permission. For instance, if there was gunfire going on or you were seeing some sort of action or if you saw people who were just going about their business, then perhaps you would come say, "Can we have a talk to you and see what you're doing." And usually we would be taken by whoever it was you made contact with first to whoever was the local commander and invariably it was not anybody particularly high scale. And usually they talked to you and said, "Yes, you can do this, this, or this." Occasionally, they said, "No, you can't do that." But generally they seemed very cooperative because I think they thought that we, in filming the situation, would be beneficial to them, as they felt they were the victims of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically during your stay, did you make -- did you film any footage at all by any action of a Croatian soldier?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Well, we filmed action by Croatian soldiers. I don't think that I can remember filming a Croatian soldier actually pulling a trigger. I filmed on a number of occasions Croatian soldiers at their guns, with their guns pointed at the JNA positions. I filmed Croatian soldiers moving a mortar to another location. And I, on three or four occasions, filmed the results of what Croatian soldiers were doing, volleys of explosions that were the impacts of mortars that we couldn't see firing. I don't think I can remember actually filming a Croatian soldier actually firing, certainly not firing a mortar or even firing a machine-gun. That's not to say they didn't do it. They obviously did do it and told us they had done it, but it didn't happen in front of our cameras.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us then why you don't have such footage and yet you were in a position to film such things.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Well, I think there are a number of answers to that. The first one would be that it didn't happen with anything like the frequency of the fire power that was coming into Dubrovnik. So that would be one answer. Another answer would be that at times of artillery pieces and mortars being used, that they were well hidden. I guess those would be the two main reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say that you had footage of action by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes. That's probably slightly lost in the translation, because action can -- doesn't necessarily restrict itself to meaning shooting things. But if it's clearer, perhaps I can repeat that I don't think -- I can't recall actually filming Croatian soldiers firing their weapons, though I do know from seeing the result of it that they did. And I do know from talking to them that at times they did. But I don't think I ever filmed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever film the results of their actions? If you didn't manage to film the moment of opening fire, were you able to film the results of their artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes. And the images that we filmed were used in a number of reports, but the most obvious one would be in the footage that you've seen where they score a hit on the Zarkovica position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who allowed you to reach the positions of the Croatian army on Srdj and how you got there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The first time we went there, because we didn't know our way around and didn't know the footpaths that led up the mountain. The policeman who we had met guided us to the footpath, and he showed us the way. After that, we knew the way and we would go by ourselves. Perhaps I should say, to help explain, that we had with us a translator, so that helped in operating without having an official guide. This was a translator who had actually travelled into Dubrovnik with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this realistic for you to go on foot to a fortress, which is a military facility, from which shots are fired and which was evidently a target for the JNA in the way that you describe? Amidst war operations, in a war theatre, can you simply walk to the most important position?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: There are times when you can, and you have to judge it. We waited until quite a long period when it wasn't coming under fire, and obviously we would have changed our minds and retreated very quickly if the fighting had started again. But these are just judgements that you make. You could ask a very similar question to your question there by saying is it realistic for you to go to Dubrovnik, a place that's under siege, where there is a much larger force outside, is it realistic? It's what people in our profession do from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time, Mr. Rodic, or are you at a critical point?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can break now. I have many more questions, but I'm not at a critical point right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Davies, I regret that we must ask you to come back on Thursday when we resume at 9.00 in the morning. I hope you would be able to accommodate that. Could I mention one matter, Ms. Somers, there has now been filed the Defence submissions concerning the critical issue of the admissibility of evidence relating to matters before the 6th of December. I wonder when we might expect the Prosecution response?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were informed that the submissions were filed. We have not yet received them and we will endeavour to get them in within the normal response time for a response to said motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to eliminate the word "endeavour" from that, "we will get them in."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We certainly will get them in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a much more comfortable reaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I simply have not received them yet. I know that the Defence indicated yesterday that there were three submissions that had not made their way up to the OTP as of yet, so we are waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may be able to make some good use of tomorrow then, to that end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. We have a number of Chamber-driven issues we're responding to. May I ask just one moment of indulgence on the issue of witness order. We have a number of matters concerning witness availability of scheduled witnesses. I don't -- I believe Mr. Davies did not anticipate, of course, staying beyond today and we did not realise -- none of us was aware, I believe I speak for the Defence as well, that the Chamber would not be able to sit tomorrow. So tomorrow's witness will be Thursday and Friday. That particular witness has a very particular time constraint. Ambassador Alajbeg will address an issue. She, like all of us, has scheduling concerns, but we've tried to accommodate hers. Monday's witness, Mr. Brolund, also has very narrow scheduling time, so we anticipated Monday. With the need -- Mr. Samardzic was the next witness, actually -- excuse me, going after Ambassador Alajbeg. We are going to have to do some shuffling around at this point and ask that everyone understand that is was not anything we could anticipate. Will the Chamber want to have Mr. Davies come back immediately Thursday or -- which would then pose a problem for Ambassador Alajbeg?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take your concern is whether it would be possible to interrupt the evidence of Mr. Davies at this point to have him return at a time that is convenient to him and the flow of the hearing?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That is exactly it, if it doesn't cause any major problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, would that trouble you if Mr. Davies was delayed in his cross-examination now for a period rather than continuing on Thursday morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, Your Honour, I can agree to this. There will be a loss of continuity, but in any case we can accommodate the requests of the Prosecution. According to the schedule I have received, however, the next witness to follow Mr. Davies was not to be the ambassador, but Mr. Samardzic. So that this again upsets our preparations. If we are given a list of witnesses, we don't want this to become the rule because we have to prepare for a certain witness and then we don't want it to become the rule for the order to be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic, for your indication that you could accommodate the concern of Ms. Somers and, I understand, Mr. Davies about timetabling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the matter, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the matter of the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, and the issue there was Mr. Samardzic was scheduled for today, tomorrow and that clearly has gone by the wayside for some reasons beyond our control and in order to make sure that we can try to get the ambassador completed, we would need Thursday and Friday for her testimony, which would put Mr. Samardzic again out of order. There's very little I can do about that scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I only suggest that whenever this sort of exigency arises that you might, at the very first opportunity, inform the Defence so that they have every available chance of preparing for the change, rather than finding out somewhat late in the piece that they're to deal with a different witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And along those lines, the exhibit -- the video exhibit was submitted to the Defence on the 10th of April, 2002, and this is the first time there has been a question raised on that. We will attempt to have the complete answer. I have bits of information, but I'm afraid that two-year delay has caused us some problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will now adjourn until Thursday morning. Mr. Davies need not attend on Thursday morning and we hope we can find a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting you, Your Honour, but during the cross-examination we were talking about the film footage. Can we get a response from the OTP in connection with the provenance of the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was the subject of the comment just made by Ms. Somers. She pointed out that it was some long time ago that that was made available. Because of that, they are not immediately in a position to give the answer. And as soon as that answer is known to them, they will make it available to you I think is the position. And that will be quite obviously, I'd expect, before Mr. Davies returns to complete his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. What my learned friend has said is correct, but I have to say that the clarification of these issues arose only today during the cross-examination. But we will wait, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you then. We will adjourn until Thursday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
